title: American Farm Bureau Convention Narrowly Votes Against Research into Production of Hemp

content_html_sanitized:
CHARLOTTE, N.C.
Thursday January 15, 1998

As farmers in Canada plan for their first hemp crop in decades, delegates to the American Farm Bureau convention went on record against production of industrial hemp and even eliminated language in favor of research into it in a 198-168 vote.

Missouri Farm Bureau president Charles Kruse complained the AFB, the largest U.S. farm organization, was being linked with groups like National Organization for Reform of Marijuana Laws. "Don't take the good name of Farm Bureau and associate it with these people," Kruse urged.  "If we say we support research, we are going to continue to be used," he said.

Thus, being in favor of research means "being used" -- by people who want you to be free to grow a plant grown by George Washington. On the other hand, parroting the party line of people who would seize your farm if they found one hemp plant on it, is presumably an expression of liberation. George Orwell would have understood. Animal Farm, 1998.

Another irony is that hemp research was being supported by the Kentucky Farm Bureau for   Kentucky farmers who see it as the successor to tobacco. The Kentucky Hemp Growers Cooperative Association, which supports international research, had a booth at the trade fair held as part of the AFB convention. One delegate asked if grain research should end because it can be converted into alcohol, misused by some people.

Inasmuch as the DEA has special agents whose job it is to lie to groups considering hemp, it is remarkable that then vote was a close as it was. When the American farmers find out that Canadian farmers are making money growing hemp, the DEA will have a harder job.

Tobacco is a high-income crop, with returns that can top $1,000 an acre for growers who own ``quota'' rights to grow the crop. None of the other major U.S. crops, such as cotton, corn and soybeans, come close. Most growers have small farms, which would limit the appeal of lower-grossing crops.

There are about 124,000 farms that grow roughly 1.6 billion pounds of tobacco a year on nearly 800,000 acres.
